title: Government in One Level
objective: After this level you can explain what governments do and why nearly every society has one.
summary: Government is how a community is run: laws, order, services and taxes. The word began as Greek for steering a ship, and governments grew where people shared something vital, like Sumer's rivers.

cards.headline: "Government" began as a sailor's word. It meant steering a ship.
cards.body: It comes, through Latin, from the Greek kybernan: to steer or pilot a ship. Keep that picture. A ship full of people needs someone at the helm, and this whole skill is about who steers, how, and why the rest of the crew goes along.

cards.headline: What a government is
cards.body: Britannica defines government as the political system by which a country or community is administered and regulated. In plainer words, it's how a group of people organizes itself and decides who gets the authority to make choices for everyone. A village council and a national parliament are different sizes of the same idea: someone steering.

mascot.line: Laws, protection, services, taxes. Four jobs, one steering wheel.

cards.headline: The job list
cards.body: So what does the steering involve? Governments make laws to keep order. They defend the country and keep the peace at home, with armies, police and fire services. They provide things a society needs, like schools, health care and roads. And they raise money through taxes to pay for it all. Each of those jobs gets its own level in this chapter.

cards.fact: The first big governments grew up around shared rivers.
cards.context: While humans were few, Britannica notes, there was hardly any government. Farming changed that. In Sumer, in today's Iraq, crops depended on irrigation, and the flow of water down the Tigris and Euphrates had to be coordinated by a central authority. Once lots of people share something vital, somebody has to steer.

cards.fact: Today the United Nations has 193 member states.
cards.context: They range from giants like India to tiny Tuvalu, and each one runs its affairs through a government of its own. Governments differ enormously, as Chapter 2 will show. Having one at all is the part nearly everyone shares.

title: Why Have Rules?
objective: After this level you can explain why groups need rules, from games to countries.
summary: Rules let everyone play the same game. The Football Association formed in 1863 to set one code of rules, and in 1967 Sweden switched to driving on the right to match its neighbors.

cards.headline: Before 1863, English football had no shared rulebook. It showed.
cards.body: Schools and clubs each played their own version of the game. The Football Association's own history recalls "feverish" disputes over how it should be played. Hard to enjoy a match when the two teams disagree about what game it is.

cards.headline: One rulebook for everyone
cards.body: On 26 October 1863, clubs met at the Freemasons' Tavern in London and formed the Football Association, aiming for a definite code of rules. One founder, Ebenezer Morley, argued that football should have rules the way cricket did. Now teams who had never met could play each other by the same code. That's the first job of rules: they let strangers cooperate.

cards.headline: Left or right doesn't matter. Agreeing does.
cards.body: Countries face the same problem on a bigger field. Driving on the left works fine. So does driving on the right. The trouble starts when neighbors pick differently. Sweden drove on the left, while Denmark, Finland and Norway drove on the right, and the mismatch caused accidents for Swedes driving abroad and for visitors to Sweden.

mascot.line: Spare a thought for anyone who slept through the announcement.

cards.fact: On 3 September 1967, a whole country switched sides of the road.
cards.context: Swedes call it Dagen H, for högertrafik, right-hand traffic. Early that morning, traffic stopped, then every vehicle moved over to the right. The change had to happen everywhere at once, because a traffic rule only works when everyone follows the same one. Deciding a rule like that for a whole country is a job for Level 1's steering wheel: government.

title: Power and Authority
objective: After this level you can tell power from authority.
summary: Power is the ability to impose your will on others; authority is power people accept as legitimate. Max Weber named three kinds of authority: traditional, charismatic and legal-rational.

cards.headline: A robber and a traffic officer can both make you stop. Only one has authority.
cards.body: Both get you to do something you didn't plan to do. Yet you'd feel very differently about each. A German sociologist gave us the words for that difference, and they're some of the most useful words in politics.

cards.headline: Power: getting your way
cards.body: Max Weber, in work published in 1922, defined power as the ability to exercise your will over others. That's all it takes. The robber has power. So does a bully, or anyone with a big enough stick. Notice what the definition leaves out: whether anyone thinks you ought to have it.

cards.headline: Authority: power people accept
cards.body: Authority is accepted power: power that people agree to follow because they see it as legitimate. For Weber, being obeyed wasn't enough. The order had to be accepted as valid. You wave back at the traffic officer; you don't wave back at the robber. Same stop, very different reason.

mascot.line: Next time someone says "because I said so", ask which of Weber's three they're using.

title: What a Law Is
objective: After this level you can explain what makes a rule a law.
summary: A law is a rule a community recognizes as binding, enforced by a controlling authority. Around 1750 BCE, Hammurabi of Babylon set 282 rulings in stone, written as if-then laws.

cards.headline: About 3,800 years ago, a king had his laws carved into stone.
cards.body: Around 1750 BCE, Hammurabi of Babylon had 282 legal rulings engraved on a black stone slab more than 2.25 meters tall. You can see it today in the Louvre in Paris. Why go to all that trouble? Because it shows what turns a rule into a law.

cards.headline: Rules versus laws
cards.body: Your household might ban shoes indoors. That's a rule, but not a law. Britannica describes law as the rules of conduct that a community recognizes as binding, enforced through a controlling authority. Two things make the difference: the whole community is bound by it, and an authority (Level 3's accepted power) stands ready to enforce it.

cards.headline: If this, then that
cards.body: Hammurabi's laws follow one pattern: if someone does this, then that follows. Law 196 is the famous one: if a man puts out another man's eye, his eye shall be put out. An eye for an eye. Every law is a consequence spelled out in advance, not made up after the fact.

mascot.line: Written down, public and enforced: a big step. Fair to everyone: a later chapter's story.

cards.fact: The code invited wronged people to come and read it.
cards.context: Its closing words tell anyone oppressed who has a case at law to stand before the king's image and read the inscription. A law everyone can read is a law everyone can point to. Equal for all, though? Not quite. Penalties varied with the offender's social status.

title: Public Services
objective: After this level you can name the services governments provide, like clean water and schools.
summary: Governments provide public services like schools, transport, police and fire. Public goods such as defense invite free riding, which taxes required by law overcome.

cards.headline: Turn on a tap and clean water comes out. For 1 in 4 people, it doesn't.
cards.body: In 2024, about 2.1 billion people still lacked safely managed drinking water, according to WHO and UNICEF. Services like this are easy to forget, right up until they're missing.

cards.headline: Services for everyone
cards.body: Public services are the things government provides for its people, usually open to all and paid for with taxes. Think public schools, buses and trains, the mail, police and fire departments, and food, housing and health care for people in need. Your walk to school or work probably passes half a dozen of them before you've had breakfast.

cards.headline: Why not just buy them?
cards.body: Some things are hard to sell one customer at a time. Economists call them public goods: it's hard to stop anyone using them, and one person's use doesn't leave less for others. National defense is the classic case. It protects you whether you paid or not. So why pay? Letting others pay while you enjoy the benefit is called free riding.

mascot.line: Free riding: great for one person, terrible if everyone tries it.

cards.fact: Free riders are beaten by a rule that everyone chips in.
cards.context: If people agree through the political process to pay taxes, the law can require everyone to contribute, and the public good gets made. It's Level 2's lesson again: a rule works when everybody follows the same one. How those taxes work is the next level.

title: Paying for It
objective: After this level you can explain how taxes fund government.
summary: Taxes are compulsory, unrequited payments on what people earn, buy and own. In 2024 they averaged 34.1% of GDP across OECD countries, from 18.3% in Mexico to 45.2% in Denmark.

cards.headline: A bus fare buys you a ride. What does a tax buy you?
cards.body: You hand over money either way. But the two deals work in completely different ways, and that difference is what makes a tax a tax.

cards.headline: Compulsory and unrequited
cards.body: The OECD defines taxes as compulsory, unrequited payments to government. Compulsory: you can't opt out. Unrequited: what you get back from government isn't in proportion to what you paid. A fare buys one ride. Your taxes buy nothing in particular, and help pay for Level 5's whole list.

title: The Social Contract
objective: After this level you can explain the ideas of Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau.
summary: A social contract sets out the rights and duties of rulers and ruled. Hobbes traded freedom for protection, Locke grounded government in consent, and Rousseau in the general will.

cards.headline: You never signed a contract with your government. Some say you're in one anyway.
cards.body: A social contract is an agreement, real or imagined, between the people, or between the people and their rulers, setting out the rights and duties of each. Three thinkers used the idea to tackle one question: why obey a government at all? Each gave a different answer.

cards.headline: Hobbes: anything beats chaos
cards.body: Thomas Hobbes published Leviathan in 1651, after England's civil war. Picture life with no government, he said: a war of all against all, where life is "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short." To escape it, people hand their freedom to an all-powerful sovereign in exchange for peace and protection. His bargain: safety is worth a lot of freedom.

cards.headline: Locke: government works for you
cards.body: John Locke saw it differently. Even without government, he argued, people have natural rights to life, liberty and property. Government gets its legitimacy from the consent of the governed, and if rulers violate those rights, people may resist them. Remember Level 3's authority, power people accept? Locke made that acceptance the whole foundation.

mascot.line: Three thinkers, three bargains. Philosophers still argue over which one you'd sign.

cards.headline: Rousseau: rules we make together
cards.body: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, born in Geneva, opened The Social Contract (1762) with a famous line: "Man was born free, and he is everywhere in chains." His answer was the general will. People agree together to live by laws aimed at the common good, laws they make for themselves. Obeying those, he argued, is a kind of freedom.

title: Levels of Government
objective: After this level you can explain national, regional and local government.
summary: Government comes in layers. In Canada, the federal level handles defence, provinces run schools and hospitals, and towns handle water and waste. India's panchayats govern villages.

cards.headline: Who fixes the pothole on your street? Not your country's leader.
cards.body: Government comes in layers, from the whole country down to your town. Canada makes a tidy example: it has three levels of government, each with its own list of jobs.

cards.headline: The top layer: the whole country
cards.body: Canada's federal government handles matters like national defence, foreign affairs, currency, citizenship and passports, criminal law and the postal service. These are jobs where one answer for the whole country makes sense. Imagine every town printing its own money, or running its own army.

cards.headline: The middle and bottom layers
cards.body: Canada's provinces and territories run education, hospitals and health care, and social services. Municipal governments take the jobs outside your front door: fire protection, local police, public transit, parks, waste management, water supply and local roads. Level 5's public services, it turns out, are shared out between the layers.
cards.callout: Some responsibilities are shared between levels.

mascot.line: Three layers of government over one village. That's a lot of people steering one ship.

cards.fact: In India, even a village has its own elected government.
cards.context: In 1992, India's 73rd constitutional amendment declared panchayats, elected local councils, institutions of self-government alongside the Union and state governments. They work at three tiers: the village, the block and the district. So a farmer can have a village council, a state government and a national one, all at once.

title: Nations and States
objective: After this level you can explain the difference between a nation and a state.
summary: A nation is a people with a shared identity; a state has territory, laws and a monopoly of legitimate force. The Kurds are a nation without a state; the UK is one state of four parts.

cards.headline: Tens of millions of Kurds share a nation. They have no state of their own.
cards.body: Britannica estimated the Kurds at 36 to 46 million in the mid-2010s, living mostly in parts of Iran, Iraq, Syria and Turkey. In the modern era they have had no nation-state of their own. How can so many people share a nation but not a state? Because those are two different things.

cards.headline: Nation, state, nation-state
cards.body: A nation is a community of people who share an identity: often a culture, a language or a history. A state is a political organization with territory, laws and the means to enforce them. Put the two together and you get a nation-state. A nation lives in a sense of "us". A state lives in borders, courts and passports.

cards.headline: Weber's test for a state
cards.body: Remember Max Weber from Level 3? In 1919 he defined the state as a human community that successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a territory. Only the state gets to use force, through police and courts, and people accept that it's allowed to. It's Level 3's authority, stretched across a whole country.

cards.fact: Nations and states rarely line up neatly.
cards.context: In Britannica's words, the borders of states and the boundaries of nations usually only partly overlap. The Kurds are one nation across several states. It works the other way too: the United Kingdom is one state made of four historical parts, England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, each with its own customs and traditions.

title: Checkpoint: Why Government?

cards.headline: Why government at all? A Greek philosopher had an answer long before Hobbes.
cards.body: Aristotle said human beings are by nature political animals. We don't just happen to live in groups; living together is part of what we are. Anyone who could live entirely outside a community, he said, would be either a beast or a god.

cards.headline: First life, then the good life
cards.body: Aristotle wrote that the city-state comes into being for the sake of life, but exists for the sake of the good life. That's this chapter in one line. First, survival: Sumer's shared water, Hobbes's escape from a life that's nasty, brutish and short. Then, living well: schools, clean water and rules that let strangers play the same game.

title: Monarchy
objective: After this level you can explain how monarchies work.
summary: Monarchy means rule of one: a monarch who is head of state, usually by inheritance. Malaysia elects its ruler; Louis XIV claimed absolute power by divine right.

cards.headline: Malaysia's king changes every five years. His fellow rulers elect him.
cards.body: Malaysia's head of state, officially the paramount ruler, is elected from among nine hereditary state rulers for a five-year term. That makes him unusual. In most monarchies, nobody votes for the monarch at all. So what makes a monarchy a monarchy?

mascot.line: No CV, no interview. For most thrones, the only application form is a birth certificate.

cards.headline: Rule of one
cards.body: The name gives it away. Monarchy comes from the Greek monarkhia, literally "ruling of one". Britannica defines it as a system based on the undivided rule of a single person. That person, the monarch, is head of state and usually gets the job by heredity. You don't apply for a throne. You're born next in line for it.

cards.headline: Why people went along with it
cards.body: Remember Weber's three roots of authority from Level 3? A monarch who inherits the throne was his example of traditional authority: power accepted because things have always been done this way. Many monarchs had something extra on their side. Britannica notes that successful and popular monarchs were believed to have a sacred right to rule.

cards.fact: Louis XIV of France is the textbook absolute monarch.
cards.context: Absolutism means unlimited, centralized authority, held especially by a monarch. Louis XIV, who reigned from 1643 to 1715, is Britannica's most familiar example. Its favorite defense was the divine right of kings: kings got their authority from God, so they answered to no one on Earth. That's more than seven decades of answering to no one.

title: Kings Who Reign but Do Not Rule
objective: After this level you can explain constitutional monarchy.
summary: In a constitutional monarchy the monarch is a symbolic head of state who reigns but does not govern. Sweden made its King's role entirely ceremonial in 1974; Japan's Emperor is a symbol.

cards.headline: Sweden has a king. He has no political power at all.
cards.body: Under Sweden's 1974 Instrument of Government, the King is still head of state, but he has no political power; his role is entirely ceremonial. A king who can't govern sounds like a contradiction. It's actually one of the most common kinds of monarchy.

cards.headline: Reigns, but does not govern
cards.body: Britannica defines constitutional monarchy as a system where a monarch shares power with a constitutionally organized government and acts as a symbolic head of state. The French politician Adolphe Thiers put it in five words: the king "reigns but does not govern." Not every king liked the idea. France's Louis-Philippe, who took the throne in 1830, refused to settle for that symbolic role.

cards.fact: Sweden gave up royal power in two big steps.
cards.context: In 1809, Sweden abolished royal absolutism: the King and the Riksdag, Sweden's parliament, were meant to share power. The 1974 Instrument of Government finished the job. The King stayed head of state, with a role that is entirely ceremonial. Level 11's Louis XIV would have found the job description baffling.

cards.headline: Japan's Emperor: a living symbol
cards.body: Japan's constitution makes the Emperor "the symbol of the State and of the unity of the people" and gives him no powers related to government. Britannica lists Japan alongside the United Kingdom, Belgium, Norway and Thailand as constitutional monarchies. So a crown can mean very different things: Louis XIV's unlimited power, or a symbol a whole country shares.

title: Dictatorship
objective: After this level you can explain dictatorships and how they keep power.
summary: A dictatorship is absolute power without effective limits, kept by force, terror and propaganda. Rome's dictator was a six-month emergency job; totalitarian states want all of life.

cards.headline: In ancient Rome, "dictator" was a job with a six-month limit.
cards.body: The Roman Republic appointed a dictator only in a crisis: a temporary magistrate with extraordinary powers, for at most six months. Then the job ended. Britannica's verdict on the modern kind is blunt: today's dictators resemble ancient tyrants, not ancient dictators.

cards.headline: Power with no brakes
cards.body: Britannica defines dictatorship as government in which one person or a small group holds absolute power without effective constitutional limits. The Roman version had brakes built in: a crisis to solve and a clock running. The modern version removes them. Nothing on the list can actually stop the ruler, and no deadline sends him home.

cards.headline: How dictators hold on
cards.body: Modern dictators typically take power by force or fraud, Britannica notes, then keep it through intimidation, terror and the suppression of basic civil liberties. They also use mass propaganda to keep public support. Put that in Level 3's terms. Fear gives them power; propaganda is the effort to make it look like authority, power that people accept.

mascot.line: An ordinary dictator wants you quiet. A totalitarian one wants your hobbies, your clubs and your thoughts too.

cards.fact: Some dictatorships want your whole life, not just your obedience.
cards.context: That's totalitarianism: government that permits no individual freedom and tries to put every part of life under the state. Benito Mussolini coined the term for Italy's fascist state: "all within the state, none outside the state, none against the state." Stalin's Soviet Union and Nazi Germany are Britannica's other classic cases.

title: Rule by the Few
objective: After this level you can explain oligarchy.
summary: Oligarchy is rule by a privileged few for their own ends. Venice's Great Council closed to a hereditary group; Michels argued every organization drifts toward rule by a few.

cards.headline: Venice called itself a republic. A closed club of families ran it.
cards.body: Over about a century from 1297, Venice's Great Council, the body where sovereignty lay, was closed to everyone outside a fixed hereditary group. From the 1390s, new families stopped getting in at all. Rule by one is monarchy. What do you call rule by a locked room of a few?

cards.headline: Rule of the few
cards.body: Oligarchy comes from the Greek oligos, "few", and arkhein, "to rule". Britannica defines it as government by the few, especially power used by a small privileged group for corrupt or selfish ends. Aristotle drew the line against aristocracy, rule by the best. When the few rule for themselves, it's oligarchy, and those few are typically the wealthy.

cards.fact: Venice's oligarchy lasted into the late 18th century.
cards.context: Its head of state, the doge, had immense prestige but was increasingly bound by his councils. Real power sat with the Great Council, and the Great Council belonged to the old families. Stable? For centuries. Open? Only if you were born into the right family.

mascot.line: Next time your group chat "votes" on a plan, count how many people actually chose it.

cards.headline: The iron law
cards.body: In the early 20th century, the sociologist Robert Michels made a bolder claim. His iron law of oligarchy says every organization, even one committed to democratic ideals, ends up ruled by an elite few. Leaders gain expertise, central authority and control of the bureaucracy and resources, and use them to dominate the members. Think of any club you've joined. Who actually decides?

title: Rule by Religion
objective: After this level you can explain theocracy.
summary: Theocracy is government by divine guidance or divinely guided officials. The pope holds every branch of power in Vatican City; Iran's supreme leader is a jurist above an elected president.

cards.headline: The world's smallest country announces its new ruler with smoke.
cards.body: When cardinals elect a pope in the Sistine Chapel, they burn the ballots. Black smoke means no decision yet. White smoke means a new pope. And the winner doesn't only lead a church. He runs a country, with every branch of its government in his hands.

cards.headline: Government by divine guidance
cards.body: Theocracy comes from the Greek theokratia, "rule of God", a word attributed to the historian Josephus. Britannica defines it as government by divine guidance or by officials regarded as divinely guided. Often the leaders are clergy and the law rests on religious law. Level 11's divine right put God behind a king. Theocracy puts religion at the center of the state itself.

mascot.line: Smallest country, biggest job description: lawmaker, executive and top judge, all in one.

cards.fact: In Vatican City, one person holds all three powers.
cards.context: At 0.44 square kilometers, Vatican City is the world's smallest fully independent state. The pope holds absolute executive, legislative and judicial powers there: he makes the laws, carries them out and judges them. He gets the job by election. Cardinals under 80 vote, and a winner needs a two-thirds majority.

cards.headline: Iran: a religious leader above elected offices
cards.body: Britannica names three present-day theocracies: Saudi Arabia, Iran and the Vatican. Iran mixes religious and elected offices. Since 1979, its head of state has been a supreme leader, a jurist of Islamic law chosen by the Assembly of Experts, whose members are directly elected every eight years. Iran's president and legislature are directly elected too, but the supreme leader can approve or dismiss the president and commands the armed forces.

title: Direct Democracy
objective: After this level you can explain government where citizens vote on everything themselves.
summary: In direct democracy citizens decide issues themselves, as in the Swiss Landsgemeinde and New England town meetings. Large states make it hard, so it mostly works inside representative systems.

cards.headline: Once a year, voters in two Swiss cantons make their laws by raising a hand.
cards.body: In the cantons of Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden, voters gather in the open air for the Landsgemeinde and vote on laws and taxes by a show of hands. No representatives in between. Just you, your neighbors and your right arm.

cards.headline: Cutting out the middle
cards.body: That's direct democracy: citizens make the decisions themselves instead of electing officials to decide for them. Britannica puts the contrast simply. In a representative democracy you vote for people; in a direct democracy you often vote on the issue itself. It's the closest thing to Level 7's Rousseau in practice: laws people make together, for themselves.

cards.fact: New England towns govern themselves the same way.
cards.context: A town meeting is an assembly of a town's qualified voters. Together they elect officials and school boards, and debate and vote on taxes and spending. Imagine your town's budget decided not by a council but by whoever turns up, one hand at a time.

cards.headline: The catch: size
cards.body: So why doesn't every country work this way? Britannica notes the long-standing argument that direct democracy can't work across the space and time of large modern states. Picture a whole country trying to fit into one town square. Today it mostly lives inside representative systems, as specific tools rather than the whole machine. And the square has another price: critics complain a secret ballot is impossible when everyone can see your hand.

title: Republics
objective: After this level you can explain representative government.
summary: A republic, from res publica, is ruled by representatives of the citizens, with no hereditary monarch. Madison argued representation lets self-government reach a large country.

cards.headline: In 509 BCE, Rome swapped its king for two officials elected every year.
cards.body: Britannica dates the Roman Republic from 509 BCE, when the Romans replaced their monarchy with elected magistrates. At the top stood two consuls, elected each year. And the Romans gave their new state a name you still use.

cards.headline: The public thing
cards.body: That name was res publica, Latin for "the public thing", and it gave us the word republic. Britannica defines a republic as a state ruled by representatives of the citizen body. Today the word is used for any government whose head of state isn't a hereditary monarch. The idea in one line: the state belongs to the public, not to a royal family.

mascot.line: Direct democracy: everyone in the room. Republic: everyone chooses who goes in the room.

cards.headline: Why send representatives?
cards.body: Level 16 left a problem: a whole country won't fit in one square. In Federalist No. 10, in 1787, James Madison offered an answer. A republic, he wrote, delegates government to a small number of citizens elected by the rest, so it can stretch over far more people and territory than a pure democracy. He also hoped representatives would "refine and enlarge the public views". Representation is how self-government scales up.

cards.fact: A republic isn't automatically a democracy, and a democracy needn't be a republic.
cards.context: Res publica once covered any non-tyrannical state, oligarchies included. Level 14's Venice called itself a republic while a closed set of families ran it. And Level 12's Sweden became a parliamentary democracy with its King still on the throne. The label tells you there's no hereditary monarch in charge. It doesn't tell you who really decides.

title: Federal or Unitary?
objective: After this level you can explain how power can be split between the center and the regions.
summary: Federal systems split power between center and regions under a hard-to-change constitution; unitary states keep it at the center and delegate it, as the UK does with Scotland.

cards.headline: The United States is federal. Yet each of its states, inside, is unitary.
cards.body: Britannica points it out: the federal United States is made of states that each run as unitary governments, with counties and cities created by state law. How can one country be both? Because federal and unitary describe how power is shared out across the map, and you can do it differently on each floor.

cards.headline: Federal: power split by contract
cards.body: Federalism unites separate states or regions in one system while each keeps its own integrity. The split is usually written into a constitution that can be changed only by extraordinary procedures, so neither level can simply grab the other's powers. The United States, Switzerland, Canada, Australia, Germany, India and Brazil work this way. Level 8's Canadian provinces running schools and hospitals? That's federalism at work.

cards.headline: Unitary: power on loan from the center
cards.body: In a unitary state, most or all governing power sits with the central government. It delegates authority to regions and towns and channels decisions down to them. Britannica calls France the classic example of a centralized administrative system. Local councils still exist and still matter. Their powers are simply on loan.

mascot.line: Devolved power is a bit like a borrowed bike. You ride it every day, but the owner still has the spare key.

cards.fact: The UK hands power to Scotland but stays a unitary state.
cards.context: The UK Parliament's Scotland Act 1998 set up the Scottish Parliament, which opened in 1999. Yet the UK Parliament can still legislate for all parts of the UK, including devolved areas. Britannica's summary: Britain decentralizes power in practice though not in constitutional principle. Remember Level 9's UK, one state made of four parts?

title: When Government Fails
objective: After this level you can explain what happens when a state collapses.
summary: A failed state loses control of its territory and the monopoly of legitimate force and can barely provide services. Somalia collapsed in 1991; the Fragile States Index tracks the pressures.

cards.headline: In 1991, Somalia's government fell. No government replaced it.
cards.body: That year President Mohamed Siad Barre was overthrown in a popular uprising. What followed, in Britannica's words, was state collapse under rival warlords, and more than three decades of civil war. Every kind of government in this chapter assumes a state that works. What happens when it doesn't?

cards.headline: Flunking Weber's test
cards.body: Britannica describes a failed state as one that can't project authority over its territory and people, or protect its borders. It can't keep a monopoly on the legitimate use of violence, and it provides only minimal public services. Remember Weber's definition of the state from Level 9: the monopoly of legitimate force within a territory. A failed state is what losing that monopoly looks like.

cards.headline: What failure costs
cards.body: Level 7's Hobbes imagined life without government as a war of all against all, "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short." Failed states show the real costs. Britannica lists crumbling infrastructure, flourishing corruption, and worsening basic measures such as infant mortality and literacy. Level 5's public services, it turns out, are what a working state quietly delivers every day.

cards.fact: Failure comes in degrees, and it can be spotted early.
cards.context: The Fund for Peace's Fragile States Index scores countries on twelve indicators, including state legitimacy, public services, and refugees and internally displaced people. The point isn't a pass-or-fail stamp. It's spotting the pressures pushing a state toward the brink, while there's still time to act.

title: Democracy's Roots
objective: After this level you can trace democracy from Athens to today.
summary: Democracy is Greek for rule by the people. Cleisthenes' Athens (508-507 BCE) tied rights to where you lived, though only free adult men took part; Lincoln restated the idea in 1863.

cards.headline: Every time you say "democracy", you're speaking ancient Greek.
cards.body: The word is a two-part sentence about who's in charge, and it has been in use for about 2,500 years. This level follows it from the city that coined it to a famous speech that put it into plain English.

cards.headline: People plus rule
cards.body: Democracy comes from the Greek demokratia, coined in the middle of the 5th century BCE from demos, "people", and kratos, "rule". Level 1 said government is about who gets the authority to decide for everyone. Democracy's answer is right there in the name: the people do.

cards.headline: Cleisthenes redraws the map
cards.body: In Athens, the statesman Cleisthenes is regarded as the founder of democracy. His reforms, approved in 508–507 BCE, changed one big thing: political rights would depend on your deme, or township, not your family or clan. Ten new local tribes replaced four old kinship ones. Suddenly what counted was your address, not your grandfather.

cards.fact: Athens' "people" meant only its free adult men.
cards.context: Britannica notes that democracy was historically a minority affair: in ancient Athens, all free adult males. Women, enslaved people and resident foreigners were excluded. The demos was real, but it was a club with a strict door policy.

mascot.line: Of, by, for. Three tiny words, and the old Greek one still fits inside them.

cards.headline: Of, by and for the people
cards.body: On 19 November 1863, dedicating a cemetery for Union soldiers at Gettysburg, Abraham Lincoln resolved that "government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth." That's demokratia unpacked into three little phrases: the people own it, run it, and are its point.

title: Magna Carta and Limits on Kings

summary: On 15 June 1215 King John agreed to Magna Carta, putting the king under the law: no imprisonment without lawful judgment, no tax without consent, and 25 barons to enforce it.

cards.headline: In 1215, England's rebel barons made their king promise to obey the law.
cards.body: Chapter 1 showed rulers making laws, all the way back to Hammurabi. This level is about the harder trick: making a ruler keep them. It happened in a meadow by the Thames, and it wasn't the king's idea.

cards.headline: A king under pressure
cards.body: On 15 June 1215, at Runnymede beside the River Thames, King John agreed to Magna Carta, Latin for "Great Charter", under pressure from rebellious barons. Its 63 clauses wrote down the liberties of "free men". Britannica sums up the big idea: the sovereign is subject to the rule of law. The king makes laws, and the laws bind the king.

mascot.line: Clause 39 is the one people still quote. "Lawful judgment" is doing a lot of work there.

cards.headline: A charter with teeth

If the king broke it, they could seize his castles, lands and possessions until he made amends. A king who can lose his castles for breaking the rules is a king with limits.

title: Parliaments
objective: After this level you can explain how parliaments work.
summary: A parliament is a place for talking that makes laws, controls taxes and holds government to account. Iceland's Althing (about 930) has one chamber; the UK's Parliament has two.

cards.headline: Iceland's Althing met at the same site for more than eight centuries.
cards.body: Iceland's Althing was founded at Thingvellir around 930 and met there until 1798. Britannica counts it among the oldest national parliaments in the world. So what exactly is a parliament for? The name gives the first clue.

cards.headline: A place for talking
cards.body: Parliament comes from the Old French parlement, "a speaking, talk", from parler, "to speak". That's the core of it: a room (or, in Iceland's case, a site) where a country's representatives argue things out in the open before anything is decided. Kings could simply give orders; a parliament has to talk things through first.

mascot.line: Make the laws, hold the purse, question the government. That's the job description.

cards.headline: Laws, money, scrutiny

Its elected House of Commons has the sole right to impose taxes and decide funding for government services: Level 22's "no tax without consent", now given by elected members. cards.headline: Prime ministers: chosen by parliament
cards.body: In a parliamentary system, the head of government, the prime minister, is selected by the legislature. Usually the party or coalition with the most seats forms the government. And what parliament gives, it can take away: a prime minister can be removed whenever they lose the confidence of a majority of parliament. That's the 1979 story.

cards.headline: Presidents: elected for a fixed term

title: Separation of Powers
objective: After this level you can explain the three branches of government.
summary: Separation of powers splits making, carrying out and judging laws among separate bodies. Montesquieu (1748) warned power tends to be abused; Bagehot (1867) noted Britain nearly fuses two of the three.

cards.headline: In 1748, a French thinker warned: anyone given power tends to abuse it.
cards.body: In The Spirit of Laws, Montesquieu wrote that every man invested with power is apt to abuse it, and to carry his authority as far as it will go. His fix wasn't to hunt for better rulers. It was to cut power into pieces.

cards.headline: Three jobs, three sets of hands
cards.body: Separation of powers divides government's three functions among separate, independent bodies: legislative (making laws), executive (carrying them out) and judicial (judging disputes about them). The aim, Britannica says, is to limit arbitrary excesses by government. Picture a game where one person writes the rules, enforces them and referees every dispute. You'd never win a call.

mascot.line: Not "find a good ruler" but "make sure no ruler has everything". A very different bet.

cards.headline: Montesquieu's warning
cards.body: When the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person or body, Montesquieu wrote, there can be no liberty. Nor can there be liberty if the judicial power isn't separated from the other two. A ruler who makes the law, enforces it and judges it doesn't need to break any rules. They are the rules.

cards.headline: Britain's "efficient secret"
cards.body: Remember Level 24: a prime minister is chosen by parliament. In The English Constitution (1867), Walter Bagehot called the efficient secret of Britain's system the close union, the nearly complete fusion, of executive and legislative powers. The link is the Cabinet: a committee of the legislature selected to be the executive. So separation comes in degrees, not one blueprint.

cards.headline: Power checking power

title: Political Parties
objective: After this level you can explain why political parties form.
summary: Washington warned against parties in 1796, yet they formed: groups organized to win and use power that recruit candidates, organize voters, govern and oppose. Whig and Tory began as insults.

cards.headline: George Washington warned against political parties. Parties formed anyway.
cards.body: In his Farewell Address of 1796, Washington warned against "the baneful effects of the spirit of party". Yet in the 19th century, modern parties took shape across Europe and the United States. If they're so worrying, why do they keep appearing?

cards.headline: What a party is
cards.body: Britannica defines a political party as a group of persons organized to acquire and exercise political power. Remember Level 3: Weber called power the ability to exercise your will over others. A party is people deciding to pursue that together, in the open, under one name.

cards.headline: Why parties form
cards.body: One candidate can't run a country, and one lawmaker alone can't pass much. Parties recruit candidates, organize voters at elections, form governments and keep them going. And the side that loses doesn't vanish: parties give those out of power an organized opposition. Those are jobs somebody has to do, and parties grew up doing them.

mascot.line: Being called a bandit and replying "great, that's our name now" is a very political move.

cards.fact: Britain's first party names began as insults.
cards.context: "Whig" and "Tory" were terms of abuse, hurled in 1679 during the fight over excluding James, Duke of York, from the throne. Tory first meant an Irish outlaw or robber; Whig probably came from a Scottish word for a horse drover. The parties then adopted the insults as their own names.

title: A Free Press
objective: After this level you can explain why a free press matters in a democracy.
summary: Sweden's 1766 law, regarded as the first for press freedom, ended censorship and opened official documents. A free press informs the people who steer; Carlyle called it a Fourth Estate.

cards.headline: In 1766, Sweden became the first country to free its press by law.
cards.body: On 2 December 1766, Sweden's parliament, the Riksdag, passed what is regarded as the world's first law supporting freedom of the press and freedom of information. What does a free press have to do with democracy? Quite a lot.

cards.headline: Two freedoms in one law
cards.body: Sweden's act abolished censorship of printed publications, including imports (academic and theological works were the exception). It also guaranteed public access to documents drawn up by government agencies. Two ideas in one law: you can publish without asking permission, and you can see what your government writes down.

mascot.line: Voting without news is like reviewing a restaurant you've never eaten at.

cards.headline: You can't steer blind
cards.body: Britannica defines press freedom as the right of media outlets to report news without government control, and it matters because it gives people informed access to information and opinions about political matters. Remember Level 1's ship: government means steering. In a democracy the people are meant to steer, and nobody steers well in the dark.

cards.headline: The Fourth Estate
cards.body: Thomas Carlyle wrote that Burke said there were Three Estates in Parliament, "but, in the Reporters' Gallery yonder, there sat a Fourth Estate more important far than they all." The name stuck: the press is still called the Fourth Estate. Carlyle's point: the people reporting on Parliament held a power of their own.

title: Protest and Free Speech
objective: After this level you can explain the right to speak out and protest.
summary: Speakers' Corner lets anyone speak lawfully, after 1866's torn-down railings. The 1966 UN Covenant protects expression (Article 19) and peaceful assembly (Article 21), within necessary laws.

cards.headline: In one corner of a London park, anyone can stand up and talk about anything.
cards.body: It's Speakers' Corner in Hyde Park. You can turn up unannounced and speak on any subject, as long as the police consider your speech lawful. That last condition is this whole level in miniature: a right to speak out, with edges.

cards.headline: Won by pulling down railings
cards.body: In 1866 the government suppressed a Reform League meeting in Hyde Park that was demanding a wider right to vote. Finding the park locked, demonstrators tore up hundreds of yards of railings to get in. Then in 1872 the Parks Regulation Act set out rules under which people could meet and speak freely in the park. The protest came first; the rules followed.

cards.headline: Written into international law
cards.body: The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, adopted by the UN General Assembly on 16 December 1966, protects both halves of protest. Article 19: everyone has the right to hold opinions without interference, and to freedom of expression, including to seek, receive and impart information and ideas. Article 21: "The right of peaceful assembly shall be recognized." Speaking out, and gathering to do it.

mascot.line: A right with edges is still a right. The argument is always about where the edges go.

cards.headline: The edges
cards.body: Neither right is unlimited. Restrictions must be set by law and be necessary, for example to respect the rights or reputations of others, or to protect national security, public order, or public health or morals. Notice the key word in Article 21: peaceful. And remember Level 4: a law is a rule the community recognizes as binding. Here, law is what marks where the megaphone stops.

title: What a Constitution Is
objective: After this level you can explain what a constitution does.
summary: A constitution is a state's supreme law: it sets up government, divides and limits power, and protects rights. The US's is one document; the UK's is a collection.

cards.headline: Britain has a constitution. Just don't ask to borrow a copy.
cards.body: In the United States, the constitution is one specific written document. In the United Kingdom, it's a collection of documents, statutes and traditional practices that are generally accepted as governing political matters. There's no single booklet to hand you. So what makes something a constitution at all?

cards.headline: The rules for making rules
cards.body: Level 4 defined a law as a rule the whole community is bound by. A constitution sits one floor up. Britannica calls it the body of doctrines and practices that form the fundamental organizing principle of a state. International IDEA puts it more simply: a constitution is the supreme law of a country, and ordinary laws are made inside the framework it sets. It's the rulebook for the people who write the rulebooks.

mascot.line: Build it, share it out, fence it in. That's a constitution's whole to-do list.

cards.headline: Three jobs in one document
cards.body: What does that top-floor law actually do? Constitutions establish the system of government: who holds which office. They distribute and constrain power, so no office can do whatever it likes. And they protect the rights of citizens. In short, a constitution tells a government what it may do, and just as importantly, what it may not.

cards.fact: Aristotle's simplest definition of a constitution: "the arrangement of the offices" in a state.
cards.context: Remember Level 10's Aristotle, who called humans political animals? Britannica traces the whole idea of a constitution back to the ancient Greeks, and especially to him. By his definition, Britain qualifies easily. Its offices are arranged, with a collection of statutes, documents and practices saying how. The arrangement just isn't printed in one place.

cards.headline: Paper is the easy part
cards.body: Here's the catch. Britannica notes that virtually every state claims to have a constitution, but not every government conducts itself in a consistently constitutional manner. Writing "power is limited" on parchment doesn't limit anything by itself. The words only bite when the people holding power actually follow them.

title: The U.S. Constitution
objective: After this level you can explain the oldest written national constitution still in use.
summary: Signed in Philadelphia in 1787 to replace the Articles of Confederation, the U.S. Constitution is the oldest written national constitution in use: seven articles, a supreme law.

cards.headline: The oldest written national constitution still in use fits on four pages.
cards.body: Britannica calls the U.S. Constitution the oldest written national constitution in use. All four pages of the original are on permanent display at the National Archives. And it opens with three words that say whose document it is: "We the People."

cards.headline: Plan B, written in one summer
cards.body: It wasn't the country's first try. It replaced the Articles of Confederation, which had denied the national government essential powers like direct taxation. Remember Level 6? A government that can't tax is a ship with no fuel. So in the summer of 1787, delegates in Philadelphia drafted something stronger, and 39 of them signed it on 17 September 1787.

cards.headline: Seven articles, one supreme law
cards.body: The Constitution has seven articles. Article I gives lawmaking power to Congress, Article II gives executive power to a President, and Article III gives judicial power to a Supreme Court and lower courts. Then Article VI adds the line that makes it a constitution in Level 31's sense: it shall be "the supreme Law of the Land."

mascot.line: Notice who's doing the establishing in that sentence. Not a king. The people.

cards.headline: Nine states to switch it on
cards.body: Signing wasn't enough. Article VII said the Constitution needed ratifying by nine states, and once they had, it took effect in 1789. Now look at that opening again. Level 7's Locke grounded government in the consent of the governed. This document begins with "We the People" and says they "do ordain and establish" it.

cards.fact: Its first ten amendments, ratified in 1791, are called the Bill of Rights.
cards.context: The original articles mostly build the machinery of government. The Bill of Rights added guarantees for people, starting with the First Amendment: "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion," plus protections for speech, the press, assembly and petition. Several levels in this chapter start right there.

title: Changing a Constitution
objective: After this level you can explain how constitutions are amended.
summary: Constitutions change by amendment, which most make harder than ordinary lawmaking. A 1789 US pay amendment was ratified in 1992 thanks to a student's C-grade paper.

cards.headline: In 1982 a student got a C on a paper. Then he helped amend the Constitution.
cards.body: Gregory Watson, a sophomore at the University of Texas at Austin, wrote about a congressional pay amendment proposed back in 1789. Congress had never set a deadline for ratifying it, he argued, so it was still pending. His professor wasn't convinced and gave him a C. So Watson started writing to state lawmakers.

cards.headline: Harder than a law, on purpose
cards.body: Constitutions must be able to change, but most make amending harder than passing an ordinary law. The usual hurdles: a supermajority in the legislature, a referendum, a double decision (sometimes with an election in between), or approval by the states or regions. Why bother? Too rigid, and needed reforms get stuck. Too flexible, and whoever holds power can wear away the rights and institutions the constitution protects.

mascot.line: Moral of the story: always check whether your homework is still pending ratification.

cards.headline: The American hurdle, and a two-century wait
cards.body: Under Article V, an amendment needs two-thirds of both houses of Congress (or a convention) to propose it and three-fourths of the states to ratify it. That bar has been cleared just 27 times. Watson's letters helped: the pay amendment, proposed on 25 September 1789, was ratified on 7 May 1992 as the 27th Amendment. In 2017 his university changed his grade to an A.

cards.headline: Some countries ask everyone
cards.body: Other countries set the bar differently. Some require a referendum for every amendment, however small: Australia, Denmark, Ireland and Japan among them. In Ireland, parliament passes a change the way it passes an ordinary law, and then a majority of voters must approve it. Remember Level 8's village panchayats? India gave them their status through its 73rd constitutional amendment in 1992.

cards.fact: More than 70 constitutions have parts that can't be amended at all.
cards.context: Examples include basic human rights in Germany. These locks are often the result of past traumas: countries coming out of conflict or dictatorship want to make sure the old oppression can never come back, not even through a perfectly legal vote.

title: Human Rights
objective: After this level you can explain the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
summary: On 10 December 1948 the UN adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, with no votes against. Nonbinding at first, it inspired treaties and constitutions.

cards.headline: In 1948 the world wrote down rights for everyone. Not one country voted no.
cards.body: On 10 December 1948, meeting in Paris, the UN General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Eight countries abstained. None voted against. The promise was right there in the name: rights not for the citizens of one country, but for everyone.

cards.headline: A committee from many backgrounds
cards.body: The drafting was chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt. France's René Cassin wrote the first draft, with Lebanon's Charles Malik and China's Peng Chung Chang among the key figures. The Commission's 18 members came from various political, cultural and religious backgrounds. Getting that room to agree on one list was the achievement.

cards.headline: Article 1, in one breath
cards.body: The Declaration has 30 articles, and the first sets the tone: "All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights." Article 2 says the rights belong to everyone, without distinction of race, colour, sex, language, religion or opinion. Article 3 promises life, liberty and security of person. Sound familiar? Level 7's Locke argued for natural rights to life, liberty and property.

mascot.line: No teeth at first. Treaties and constitutions supplied them.

cards.headline: A standard, not a statute
cards.body: The UN proclaimed it as a common standard of achievement for all peoples and all nations. It wasn't a binding law, and Britannica notes that its nonbinding status was first seen as a major weakness. Then it spread. In 1966 the UN adopted two covenants, on civil and political rights and on economic, social and cultural rights. The Declaration has inspired more than seventy human rights treaties, and many countries wrote it into their constitutions.

cards.fact: The Declaration is available in more than 500 languages.
cards.context: A common standard for all peoples only works if people can read it. That's the point of all those translations: whatever your language, the chances are good you can read Article 1 in it.

title: Freedom of Religion
objective: After this level you can explain freedom of religion and belief.
summary: Freedom of religion covers belief, which can't be limited, and practice, which can be, but only for a few listed reasons. Countries arrange religion and state differently.

cards.headline: You can believe whatever you like. Acting on it is where the rules begin.
cards.body: Article 18 of the Universal Declaration gives everyone freedom of thought, conscience and religion. That includes the freedom to change your religion or belief, and to show it in teaching, practice, worship and observance. Two halves, then: what you believe, and what you do about it. International law treats them very differently.

cards.headline: Believing: no limits allowed
cards.body: The UN Human Rights Committee says no limitations are permitted on the freedom to have or adopt a religion or belief of your choice. The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) adds that no one may be coerced in a way that would impair that freedom. A government can't make it illegal to believe something. Your mind is the one room it never gets a key to.

cards.headline: Practising: limits, but only a few
cards.body: Showing your religion is different, because it can affect other people. Under ICCPR Article 18, it may be limited, but only by law and only where necessary to protect public safety, order, health or morals, or the fundamental rights and freedoms of others. Think of it as a short list of permitted reasons. Any limit has to point to one of them.

The Stasi Commission and President Jacques Chirac backed it as applying laïcité, France's secularism. Human Rights Watch called it an unwarranted infringement on religious practice, arguing such symbols threatened no one's safety, order or rights. Underneath sits one question: when is a limit on practice truly necessary?

title: Privacy
objective: After this level you can explain the right to privacy.
summary: Warren and Brandeis called privacy 'the right to be let alone' in 1890. It's in the UN Declaration, built by US courts from the Bill of Rights, and extended to data by the EU.

cards.headline: In 1890, two lawyers warned that cameras were invading private life.
cards.body: "Instantaneous photographs and newspaper enterprise have invaded the sacred precincts of private and domestic life," wrote Samuel Warren and Louis Brandeis in the Harvard Law Review. Their answer was a right with a wonderfully plain name: "the right to be let alone." Swap the camera for a phone and it could have been written this morning.

cards.headline: Written into the world's list
cards.body: Level 34's Declaration took the idea global. Article 12 says no one shall be subjected to arbitrary interference with their privacy, family, home or correspondence, nor to attacks on their honour and reputation. Notice the word "arbitrary." The promise isn't that nobody may ever look. It's that nobody may pry on a whim.

cards.headline: The missing word in the U.S. Constitution
cards.body: Search the U.S. Constitution for "privacy" and you won't find it. Courts built the right from parts of Level 32's Bill of Rights, especially the First, Fourth and Fifth Amendments. The Fourth protects people "in their persons, houses, papers, and effects" against unreasonable searches and seizures, and requires warrants based on probable cause. In 1965 the Supreme Court described a "zone of privacy" formed by these guarantees.

cards.headline: Your data, your rights
cards.body: Today much of your private life is data. In the European Union, data protection is a fundamental right under Article 8 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights, and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) has applied since 25 May 2018. You can ask an organisation whether it holds personal data about you and, in some cases, have it erased: the so-called right to be forgotten.

mascot.line: Rights don't live alone. Sometimes they have to share the room.

cards.headline: When rights collide
cards.body: Privacy often has to be weighed against other things people value. The EU's right to erasure doesn't apply where processing the data is needed for freedom of expression, a legal obligation or legal claims. And Britannica points to the USA PATRIOT Act of 2001, which widened federal access to business records in terrorism investigations, as an example of the tension between privacy and national security.

title: Who Gets to Vote
objective: After this level you can explain how the right to vote expanded over time.
summary: Suffrage, the right to vote, once needed property in Britain and was denied by race in places. US amendments and the UN Declaration widened it; Austria now votes at 16.

cards.headline: For a long time, voting wasn't a right. It came with property.
cards.body: In 18th- and 19th-century Britain, you needed property or a certain income to vote. The argument was that only people with "a stake in the country" should have a voice in its public affairs. So how did the vote get from the propertied few to the rest?

cards.headline: Suffrage: who's in, who's out
cards.body: Suffrage is the right to vote, in electing public officials and, where a country allows it, on proposed laws. Every country draws a line around who has it. Some lines were drawn by race: South Africa at one time, and the Old South of the United States, did not permit their Black populations to vote. This level follows that line as it moved.

Article 21 says the will of the people shall be the basis of the authority of government, expressed in periodic and genuine elections by universal and equal suffrage, held by secret vote. Recall Level 3: authority is power people accept as legitimate. Article 21 names elections as the way that acceptance is expressed.

mascot.line: Property, race, age: each line on this card was once taken for granted.

cards.fact: In 2007 Austria lowered its voting age from 18 to 16.
cards.context: Austria's parliament says it was the first country in Europe to lower the voting age to 16 for all citizens. From property owners to 16-year-olds: the line is still moving.

cards.headline: The first country where women won the vote? New Zealand, in 1893.
cards.body: On 19 September 1893, New Zealand women were granted the vote. That made New Zealand the first self-governing country in the world to give women the vote in parliamentary elections. It didn't happen by chance.

cards.headline: 31,872 signatures and a seven-year push
cards.body: Kate Sheppard of the Women's Christian Temperance Union led a seven-year campaign: public meetings, telegrams and letters to politicians, and a steady stream of pamphlets. Its climax was the 1893 petition, with 31,872 signatures, the largest ever gathered in Australasia. It was reportedly carried to Parliament in a wheelbarrow.

title: Civil Rights
objective: After this level you can explain civil rights movements and what they won.
summary: Civil rights guarantee equal treatment under the law and usually need government action. The US movement won the 1964 and 1965 Acts; South Africa ended apartheid.

cards.headline: On 1 December 1955, a 43-year-old woman refused to give up her bus seat.
cards.body: Rosa Parks was arrested in Montgomery, Alabama, for refusing to give up her seat to a white passenger. What followed was the Montgomery bus boycott, which lasted about a year, led by an organisation that chose a young minister as its president: Martin Luther King Jr.

cards.headline: Rights that need the government to act
cards.body: Britannica defines civil rights as guarantees of equal social opportunities and equal protection under the law, regardless of race, religion or other personal characteristics. It draws a neat contrast. Civil liberties are secured by restraining government, like Level 32's First Amendment, which begins "Congress shall make no law." Civil rights usually need positive government action, often new legislation.

cards.headline: From a bus seat to a national law
cards.body: The boycott ended with a legal win: a federal court found segregation on publicly operated buses unconstitutional, and the U.S. Supreme Court affirmed it. Then came legislation. On 2 July 1964, President Lyndon B. Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act, which banned discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex or national origin in places like restaurants and hotels, and at work.

mascot.line: A right on paper and a right in practice can be a lifetime apart.

cards.headline: A promise kept 95 years late
cards.body: Remember Level 37's 15th Amendment of 1870? Southern states had long kept Black citizens from voting anyway, with tools like literacy tests. After state troopers attacked peaceful marchers in Selma, Alabama, national attention helped persuade Congress to act. The Voting Rights Act, signed on 6 August 1965, outlawed literacy tests as a condition of voting. It enforced the 15th Amendment, 95 years after its ratification.

cards.fact: South Africa's apartheid laws were repealed in the early 1990s.
cards.context: Apartheid, Afrikaans for "apartness," was formally set up in 1948. Its laws classified people by race, and pass laws controlled where nonwhite South Africans could be. After repeal under President F. W. de Klerk, the 1994 elections produced a government led by Nelson Mandela. Level 40 picks up the story.

objective: After this level you can trace a bill from idea to law.
summary: A bill is a proposed law. It passes readings and committee in both Houses, which must agree every word before Royal Assent makes it an Act; US chambers pass identical text.

cards.headline: A bill's "first reading" doesn't involve reading it.
cards.body: In the UK House of Commons, first reading is a formality: the bill's short title is read out, it's ordered to be printed, and that's it. No debate, no vote. So where does the real work happen? Follow one bill from idea to law.

cards.headline: Bill in, Act out
cards.body: A bill is a proposal for a new law, or for a change to an existing one, put before Parliament for debate. It isn't law yet. It's a draft asking permission. Only after it clears every stage and receives Royal Assent does it become an Act of Parliament. Think of the bill as the caterpillar and the Act as the butterfly.

cards.body: Both Houses must agree the exact wording. The US works the same way: the House and the Senate must pass a bill in identical form before it goes to the President to be signed. A law is born only when both chambers agree on every word.

title: Debate
objective: After this level you can explain how lawmakers debate a bill.
summary: Second reading debates a bill's principles, under rules that keep argument on ideas. The US Senate's filibuster shows debate also needs a way to end: cloture.

cards.headline: In the House of Commons, MPs aren't allowed to call each other by name.
cards.body: Instead they say things like "the honourable Member for" someone's constituency. It sounds stuffy, but the rule has a job: to guard against personality in debate. Argue with the idea, not the person. That rule is a clue to what debate is for.

cards.headline: Arguing about the big idea
cards.body: Remember second reading from Level 41? That's where the big argument happens. The Commons debates a bill's general principles: should this law exist at all? The fine print waits for committee. A second reading debate is less about commas and more about whether the whole idea deserves to go further.

mascot.line: Wrong is allowed. Liar is not. A useful rule for family dinners too.

cards.headline: Mind your language
cards.body: Debate only works if people keep talking, so some words are off limits. Alleging that another member has lied is almost always out of order. The Speaker tells a member who uses unparliamentary language to withdraw it, and refusing can get them suspended. You can say a colleague is wrong as often as you like. Just not that they're lying.

cards.headline: How do you stop a talker?
cards.body: The US Senate allows extended debate, so senators can use long speeches to delay a bill. That's a filibuster, from a Dutch word for "freebooter" and the Spanish "filibusteros": pirates raiding the Caribbean. In 1917 the Senate adopted cloture, a way to end debate with a two-thirds vote. In 1975 it lowered the bar to three-fifths of senators, usually 60 of 100. Every chamber needs an answer to one question: when does talking stop and voting start?

title: Committees
objective: After this level you can explain what committees do.
summary: Committees do lawmaking's detailed work. In Congress most bills die in committee; the rest get hearings and mark-up. In the UK, select committees also shadow each government department.

cards.headline: Want to see where laws are really made? Skip the big chamber.
cards.body: In 1885 Woodrow Wilson wrote: "Congress in session is Congress on public exhibition, whilst Congress in its committee-rooms is Congress at work." The speeches are the show. The committee room is the workshop.

cards.headline: Where bills go to wait
cards.body: No chamber can study every bill together, so each one is referred to a committee with its own area of policy, such as agriculture or education. And that's where most bills die. They're never reported out to the whole House or Senate. For a bill, getting introduced is easy. Getting out of committee is the hard part.

cards.headline: Hearings, then mark-up
cards.body: A bill that does get attention usually starts with a public hearing, where the committee hears witnesses representing different viewpoints. Then comes the mark-up session: members go through the bill and vote on amendments. Finally the committee reports the bill to the full chamber, or tables it, which ends the story. It's the line-by-line work Level 41's committee stage promised.

mascot.line: A committee for every department. Somebody is always taking notes.

title: The Veto
objective: After this level you can explain how a veto works.
summary: A veto, Latin for "I forbid", is an executive's power to reject a bill. The US President has 10 days to sign or veto; Congress can override by two-thirds. Override rules vary by country.

cards.headline: "Veto" is Latin for two words: "I forbid."
cards.body: In ancient Rome it was the term for a protest by a tribune of the people against a measure of the Senate or the magistrates. Presidents today still use the same word to stop a bill in its tracks. How much power does that give them?

cards.headline: Sign it or send it back
cards.body: A veto is an executive's power to reject a bill, preventing it from becoming law. In the US, the President has 10 days (Sundays excepted) to sign a bill or return it to Congress with objections. Congress can override a veto, but only by a two-thirds vote in each chamber. And if Congress adjourns so the President can't return the bill, it's a pocket veto, which can't be overridden at all.

cards.fact: Franklin D. Roosevelt vetoed 635 bills. Congress overrode 9.
cards.context: That's more vetoes than any other US president. Two-thirds of both chambers is a lot of agreement to find, and FDR's record shows it: nine overrides out of 635 tries.

mascot.line: One signature can change the math from half the room to two-thirds of it.

cards.headline: Different countries, different bars
cards.body: Override rules vary. Two-thirds is most common, in countries such as Mexico, Ghana and the Philippines. Poland needs three-fifths; Brazil needs only an absolute majority in both chambers. International IDEA points out what a veto really does: if the president backs a bill, an ordinary majority passes it. If the president opposes it, lawmakers need a supermajority.

title: Regulations
objective: After this level you can explain how government agencies write detailed rules.
summary: Laws often leave details to ministers and agencies. UK secondary legislation fills in Acts; US agencies write regulations under authority from Congress through notice and comment, which is not a vote.

cards.headline: Parliament passes the Act. Then ministers write thousands of rules under it.
cards.body: In the UK, about 3,500 statutory instruments are made each year, and only about 1,000 of them need to be considered by Parliament. They're law too. So who writes them, and who keeps them in check?

cards.headline: Filling in the details
cards.body: An Act often sets out the big idea and leaves the fine print to someone else. That fine print is secondary legislation: law made by ministers or other bodies under powers given to them by an Act of Parliament. It fills in the details that make an Act work in daily life. If the Act is the recipe's title, the regulations are the measurements.

cards.headline: Where US agencies get the power
cards.body: The US works the same way. Agencies get their authority to issue regulations from laws enacted by Congress, and they must not go beyond it. The Administrative Procedure Act of 1946 sets an open process: an agency publishes a proposed rule in the Federal Register, takes public comments, then publishes a final rule, which goes into the Code of Federal Regulations.

mascot.line: One good argument beats a thousand copies of the same one.

cards.headline: Comments count, but they're not votes
cards.body: Anyone can comment on a proposed federal rule. But it isn't a ballot: an agency may not base its final rule on how many comments are for or against. It must reason from the record. As the EPA puts it, one well-supported comment is often more informative than a thousand form letters.

title: Local Laws
objective: After this level you can explain city and town rules.
summary: Byelaws are local laws a council makes for its own area, using powers from a higher government. Canada's municipalities are "creatures" of the provinces; US states follow Dillon's Rule or home rule.

cards.headline: Your city might have a law about ear piercing.
cards.body: Leeds, in England, does. Its council's byelaws cover hairdressers and barbers, ear piercing, pleasure fairs, the employment of children and the city's parks. So who gets to make rules like these, and how far can they go?

cards.headline: Laws with a postcode
cards.body: A byelaw is a local law made by a local authority, and it applies only within that area. The council doesn't invent the power to make it: it uses powers granted by Acts of Parliament. Sound familiar? It's Level 46's delegated power again, handed down one more floor, from Parliament to the town hall.

cards.headline: Creatures of the province
cards.body: Remember Level 8's Canadian municipalities, running water supply, parks and local roads? Their power comes from above. Canada's Constitution Act, 1867 gives provinces power over municipal institutions, and courts have called municipalities "creatures" of the provincial legislature. They have only the powers provincial law gives them.

mascot.line: Ask what a city may do, and the answer starts with who gave it the power.

cards.headline: Two American answers
cards.body: US states differ on how much power to hand down. Under Dillon's Rule, from two 1868 decisions by Iowa judge John F. Dillon, a local government may act only where the state has granted it the power. Home rule, which emerged in the early 1900s, delegates broader power from the state to its towns and cities. Either way, a local law lives inside a bigger government's law.

title: Unjust Laws
objective: After this level you can explain how laws can be unjust and how they get repealed.
summary: Thinkers disagree about what to do with a law you believe is unjust. Thoreau and King argued for civil disobedience; Plato's Socrates chose to obey. The legal route out of a law is repeal.

cards.headline: In 1846, a writer spent a night in jail rather than pay a tax.
cards.body: Henry David Thoreau refused to pay his poll tax in Concord, Massachusetts, in protest against slavery and the Mexican-American War. His night in a cell opens a long argument: what should you do about a law you believe is unjust? Thinkers have given very different answers.

cards.headline: Thoreau: don't be the tool
cards.body: Thoreau turned the experience into an essay, "Resistance to Civil Government" (1849), later known as "Civil Disobedience." If a law requires you to be "the agent of injustice to another," he wrote, "then, I say, break the law." The essay went on to influence Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr.

cards.headline: King: break it openly
cards.body: In his Letter from Birmingham Jail (1963), King argued that people have a moral responsibility to obey just laws and to disobey unjust ones. But not in secret: one who breaks an unjust law, he wrote, must do so "openly, lovingly, and with a willingness to accept the penalty." He'd been arrested for parading without a permit. A permit rule is fine in itself, he argued; it becomes unjust when used to maintain segregation.

mascot.line: Thoreau, King and Socrates: three answers to one hard question. You get to weigh them.

cards.headline: Socrates: stay and obey
cards.body: In Plato's Crito, Socrates makes the opposite choice. Awaiting execution, he refuses a chance to escape, though he thinks his sentence unjust. By living in Athens all his life, he argues, he had implicitly agreed to obey its laws. Sound like Level 7's social contract? It's the same idea, told as a prison conversation.

cards.fact: South Africa's parliament repealed its race-classification law in 1991.
cards.context: The Population Registration Act of 1950 had classified all South Africans by race. It ended through the lawmaking process you've followed all chapter: a new act repealed it.
